description_full: Roper Technologies, Inc. designs and develops vertical software and technology enabled products in the United States, Canada, Europe, Asia, and internationally. Its Application Software segment offers comprehensive management, diagnostic and laboratory information management, enterprise software and information solutions, K-12 school administration, transportation management, financial and compliance management, cloud-based and integrated payment processing, campus technology and payment, and cloud-based financial analytics, performance management software, and data solutions; cloud-based software for the property and casualty insurance industry; and foodservice technologies. The Network Software segment provides cloud-based data, collaboration, and estimating automation software; electronic marketplace; visual effects and 3D content software; cloud-based software and AI-enabled analytics solutions for the life insurance and financial services industries; supply chain software; health care services and software; data analytics and information; pharmacy software solutions; and AI-enabled SaaS providing digital engagement, as well as church management and integrated giving solutions for faith-based organizations. The Technology Enabled Products segment offers ultrasound procedures accessories; dispensers and metering pumps; wireless sensor network and solutions; automated surgical scrub and linen dispensing equipment; water meters; optical and electromagnetic precision measurement systems; RFID card and credential readers; and medical devices. It distributes and sells its products through direct sales offices, manufacturers' representatives, resellers, and distributors. The company was formerly known as Roper Industries, Inc. and changed its name to Roper Technologies, Inc. in April 2015. Roper Technologies, Inc. was incorporated in 1981 and is based in Sarasota, Florida.

financial_summary: Roper Technologies, Inc. is a large-cap technology business with a $47.2B market cap on $7.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 62% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $2.5B in free cash flow — roughly 32 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.65× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.9× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.9×.
Shareholder yield is only 1.8%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 28% operating margin runs 21pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.21x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-6.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 18% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 24% over the last three months.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 6% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 31% and a beta of 0.76, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.12 vs 5y 0.72), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $274.6M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 26% in the 2022 bear market and 48% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 15% below its DCF fair value of $562, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 30%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $399 to $816 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 18.9 vs 26.7 and P/FCF 18.9 vs 25.4 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-9%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 14 covering analysts target $467 on average, 2% below the price.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.0%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It runs a 62% gross margin and converts 32% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.65x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 10.8% of revenue on R&D and 2.1% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.9x net debt to EBITDA ($297.4M of cash against $9.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.9x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.0, in the safe zone).
The current ratio of 0.52 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 62% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 13.7% over 3 years, 7.4% over 5 years and 8.2% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 10.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.06 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 66% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 10%.
Capex runs only 0.1x depreciation (0.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 37, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (14 sales, net $32.5M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.8% (1.1% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 33 consecutive years, raising it 10.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 19,400 employees, each generates about $407K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and productivity has risen 8.8% a year.
That works out to $128K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.6M (9x revenue per employee).
